extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, induction, and the philosophy/science of method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and cautions for using, combining, and interpreting approximate generalizations (probabilistic inductions), and for treating mathematical/positional truths within inductive logic. Focuses on how to evaluate probability, dependence, error accumulation, and when approximations may be treated as universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability from an established approximate generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposition 'Most A are B' has been established by sufficient induction, we may conclude that any particular A is B with a probability proportioned to the preponderance of the number of affirmative instances over the number of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where numerical precision in the data is practicable, give a corresponding degree of precision to the chances of error (e.g., if nine out of ten A are B, there is one chance in ten of error for an unknown A). This holds only within the limits of time, place, and circumstance embraced in the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit applicability of averages to observed domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities derived from an average ('Nine out of every ten A are B') only hold within the limits of time, place, and circumstances embraced in the observations and cannot be counted on for any subclass or external circumstances not included in the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply a genus-average to a particular instance known to belong to a species or under particular circumstances; the average should only be applied to cases which are neither known nor can be presumed to be other than average cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying a general average to known species/particular circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular instance i is known to belong to some species or variety of A, or is under the influence of particular circumstances, applying the average struck for the whole genus will generally be an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using the average corresponding to that species or adjusting for the particular circumstances; general averages are commonly of little use for practical guidance of individual affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averages are first-term approximations; refine by circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: General averages can only be considered as supplying the first term in a series of approximations; subsequent terms proceed on an appreciation of the circumstances belonging to the particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use additional information about the individual case to refine the initial probabilistic estimate (e.g., actuarial tables are useful for populations but not for determining an individual's life chances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joining approximate generalizations by Addition (independent corroboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two approximate generalizations are each separately applicable to the case (e.g., Most A are B; Most C are B; the thing is both A and C), combining them by Addition yields a probability greater than either alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute combined probability under an independence assumption (example: if chance an A is not B = 1/3 and chance a C is not B = 1/4, then chance something both A and C is not B = 1/3 * 1/4 = 1/12). Ensure A and C are independent in the relevant sense; if they are connected, combined probability may not increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence requirement when combining generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The computation that multiplies chances (or otherwise combines them beneficially) presupposes that the probabilities arising from the two classes are independent of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If belonging to one class increases the chance of belonging to the other, the not-Bs in each class may coincide and the joint probability may be no better than that from a single class. Check for connections that invalidate independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joining approximate generalizations by Deduction (chains) lowers probability
rubrics_metrics.description: When only one proposition is directly applicable and the second applies by virtue of the first (e.g., Most A are B; Most B are C; this is a C; therefore probably an A → probably a B), each step in such deduction diminishes the degree of probability of the inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The diminution depends on how 'fairly' the second average is distributed over the section of B that belongs to A; errors can aggregate so that after a few steps the conclusion may be worthless. Remember that a hearsay of a hearsay or marks-of-marks becomes worthless after a few removes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error accumulation across chained premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If premises are less than universal, the error of the conclusion will amount to the aggregate of the errors of all the premises (probabilities multiply/compound so that the proportion true can shrink rapidly with steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify diminution where possible (e.g., 9/10 * 8/9 * 7/8 → 7/10) and be cautious about long chains unless the premises approach universality; otherwise, the conclusion may soon 'be worth nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform approximate generalizations into universal propositions with provisos when exceptions are identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason for stopping at an approximation is inconvenience rather than impossibility, and we know the character which distinguishes cases that accord from exceptions, we may substitute the approximate proposition by a universal one with a proviso (carry the hypothesis/condition forward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording each condition or proviso enables the argument to be treated like universal reasoning, and the sum of the conditions will indicate the aggregate error affecting the conclusion. Example: 'Most persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill' → 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate propositions can be universal for mass properties (statistics/political science)
rubrics_metrics.description: In inquiries about properties of multitudes (actions of masses, fortunes of communities), what is true of most individuals is practically enough, and may be treated as true of the mass: 'what is true approximately of all individuals is true absolutely of all masses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies the use of approximate generalizations in social/political science or statesmanship, where aggregate behavior matters more than individual deviations and where indefinite duration/succession further supports treating 'most' as if 'all.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence inferred from inductive laws of succession or co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a phenomenon not directly perceived is inferred from other phenomena ascertained by induction to be connected with it, either by succession or co-existence; to prove existence, prove a connection by succession or co-existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions affirming bare existence are peculiarly easy: a single credible instance can establish existence (e.g., the discovery once of a sea-serpent would establish it). Existence, in logic, refers to phenomena or possibilities of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare resemblances via a third object when direct juxtaposition impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: When two phenomena cannot be brought into effective juxtaposition for direct comparison, compare each through a third object (the appropriate scientific process for ascertaining resemblances/differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical generalizations (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another') and physical aids (measuring rules, balances). Recognize that partial or misleading immediate perception requires minute part-by-part comparison or indirect inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics supplies independent laws of resemblance and order in place
rubrics_metrics.description: The axioms and theorems of mathematics (equality, inequality, proportionality, geometrical order) are laws of resemblance/order which are generally independent of causal laws and require separate consideration within the methods of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mathematical uniformities (true 'of all phenomena whatever') from empirical uniformities derived from laws of cause; mathematical propositions can be used as independent tools when comparing phenomena or inferring order in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary mathematical axioms are inductive truths grounded in perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental axioms of mathematics (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another' and 'Equals added to equals make equal sums') are ultimately inductive truths founded on perpetual perception and never having been found false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although treated as self-evident or instinctive, these axioms are based on simple repeated observation (induction per enumerationem simplicem) and thus fit within the inductive account of knowledge; recognize their empirical origin when relating mathematics to scientific method.
